📚 Documentation

Currently the signature of torch.addcdiv is documented to be:
addcdiv(input, value=1, tensor1, tensor2, out=None) -> Tensor

See e.g. https://pytorch.org/docs/stable/torch.html#torch.addcdiv
This can't be correct because it has positional arguments following keyword arguments, which is invalid in Python.
When I intentionally pass an invalid number of arguments, I get:
In [10]: torch.addcdiv(t, 0.1)
---------------------------------------------------------------------------
TypeError                                 Traceback (most recent call last)
<ipython-input-10-38c653649e23> in <module>
----> 1 torch.addcdiv(t, 0.1)

TypeError: addcdiv() received an invalid combination of arguments - got (Tensor, float), but expected (Tensor input, Tensor tensor1, Tensor tensor2, Number value, Tensor out)

So I guess value is optional and it should be moved to the end of the argument list.  However, I wanted to double check before putting in a PR with the fix since that means that the doctest in the docstring for addcdiv is incorrect.

@mcarilli shares with me a use case that is not handled well by the current dispatcher. He would like to provide a toggleable AMP mode that, when turned on, results in specific functions calling an AMP implementation, rather than the usual VariableType implementation. While this can be implemented using boxed fallback (#26368) it is a bit awkward, because the implementor has to write a giant if statement inside their single generic function to match out specific function cases. Instead, it would be nice if they could just override the handful of functions they want, and then fall through to the next TensorTypeId in the dispatch line.
So, our specific proposal is this:

TensorTypeId can opt into "fallback" dispatch. We maintain a set of tensor type ids with this behavior.
In ATenDispatch, before the reportError test, we add a new condition. If the tensor type id is in the fallback dispatch set, we disable the selected tensor type id (in TLS) and redispatch.

This wasn't in the original dispatch proposal, so I want to get feedback on it first.
An alternative is to used the boxed fallback dispatch to implement this passthrough behavior, but it feels like such a heavy hammer for this nail. I think it should just be supported internally.

🚀 Feature
Related: #22402
This feature proposes passing through Tensor subclasses via __torch_function__.
Desired Behaviour
Example desired behavior would be:
class MyTensor(torch.Tensor):
    _additional_attribute = "Kartoffel"

a = MyTensor([0, 1, 2, 3])
# b should be a MyTensor object, with all class attributes passed through.
b = torch_function(a)
Goals
Quoting #22402

These are potential goals that have been collected from the above referenced PRs, other PyTorch issues (referenced in the relevant sections), as well as from discussions with mainly Edward Yang, and also other PyTorch and NumPy maintainers:

Support subclassing torch.Tensor in Python
Preserve Tensor subclasses when calling torch functions on them
Preserve Tensor subclasses when calling numpy functions on them
Use the NumPy API with PyTorch tensors (i.e. NumPy API calls dispatch to torch functions)
Use the PyTorch API with torch.Tensor-like objects that are not Tensor subclasses
Reuse NumPy ufunc implementations directly from PyTorch
Allow operations on mixed array types, e.g. tensor + ndarray


Additionally, from #28361 (comment):


Preserve Tensor subclasses when calling Tensor methods
Propagating subclass instances correctly also with operators, using views/slices/etc.


Rough Sketch of Implementation
Anything with a type like a built-in tensor will bypass __torch_function__ via their fast path (although they will have a default implementation) but anything else defined by an external library will have the option to allow it.
The following code snippet shows what the default __torch_function__ on TensorBase would look like.
class Tensor:
    def __torch_function__(self, f, t, a, kw):
        if not all(issubclass(ti, TensorBase) for ti in t):
            return NotImplemented
        result = f._wrapped(*a, **kw)
        return type(self)(result)

nodes.bodyText:
Currently, DDP computes the param to bucket mapping upfront, and allreduce grads for all params in every iteration. For unused params, it will just set grad to zero. By doing this, optimizer cannot tell if a param indeed has a zero grad or it is not used in the current iteration. This could trigger convergence problems for optimizers with weight decay and momentum.
However, DDP cannot simply set grad to None for local unused parameters, as local unused parameters might be used in other processes, and hence we still need to allreduce its grad.
Proposed Solution
We could insert a header (either to every bucket or for the entire model) indicating whether a param is used or not locally in the current iteration. Then, we can allreduce/allgather this header and use that information to decide whether we should set grads to None.

Add a .fit() method to nn.Module, which trains the model using the parameters given.

nodes.bodyText:
🚀 Feature
Tensor.max() and Tensor.min() support a dim argument to reduce over a single axis. They should support multiple axes just like Tensor.sum().
Motivation
Sometimes I want to pool over all spatial dimensions, or an arbitrary set of dimensions. Currently I have to decide myself whether to loop over dimensions (and in which order), or reshape the tensor to collapse multiple dimensions into one.
Pitch
max() and min() should support a list of dimensions. In this case, the returned indices tensor would be a matrix giving the coordinates along each dimension in their given order.
Alternatives
For the specific case of max-pooling across spatial dimensions, I could use torch.nn.functional.adaptive_max_pool2d with an output size of 1.
When extending max() and min(), there are different options for the returned indices tensor, ordered from easiest to most complex implementation:

not returning any indices if there are multiple dimensions
returning a vector of indices that index into a flattened view of the dimensions to reduce (this is what adaptive_max_pool2d_with_indices does)
returning a matrix of indices that give the indices along each of the reduced dimensions, in ascending order of dimensions
returning a matrix of indices that give the indices along each of the reduced dimensions, in the given order of dimensions

The first would avoid some headaches, but cannot be undone again without breaking the signature. It would also complicate user code that has to work both with single and multiple dimensions. So that's probably not a good route.
The second would be compatible to adaptive max-pooling, but other than that, not very practical to deal with (think of advanced indexing).
The third and forth are similarly useful. Most of the time they will be equivalent. I don't really know what users would expect who provide dim in a not-ascending order.
We cannot really look at numpy for guidance -- np.max() supports multiple axes, but np.argmax() doesn't. If np.argmax() is called without specifying an axis, it will reduce over all axes and return an index into the flattened array (i.e., option 2, the one I deemed impractical).
Disclaimer: I don't need the indices anyway.
Additional context
For summation, this was suggested in #2006 and implemented in #6152.
There also is a generic multi-dimensional operators issue in #9703, but the indices warrant some extra discussion.

nodes.bodyText:
🐛 Bug
When type-promoting while assigning values using a list index, e.g. A[:, [i]] = b, where A and b are of different dtype, the assignment produces incorrect values.
To Reproduce
A = torch.ones(5, 2, dtype=torch.double)
b = torch.rand(5) 
tensor([0.5433, 0.1091, 0.3717, 0.8436, 0.4544])


# Single-column assignment works fine
A[:, 1] = b
A
tensor([[1.0000, 0.5433],
        [1.0000, 0.1091],
        [1.0000, 0.3717],
        [1.0000, 0.8436],
        [1.0000, 0.4544]], dtype=torch.float64)


# Multi-column assignment breaks, presumably b/c of type promotion
A[:, [1]] = b.unsqueeze(-1)
A
tensor([[ 1.0000e+00,  1.1426e-10],
        [ 1.0000e+00,  1.8074e-06],
        [ 1.0000e+00,  1.4630e-03],
        [ 1.0000e+00,  1.1764e-05],
        [ 1.0000e+00, 5.2145e-315]], dtype=torch.float64)


# Multi-column assignment works if no type promotion is involved
A[:, [1]] = b.double().unsqueeze(-1)
A
tensor([[1.0000, 0.5433],
        [1.0000, 0.1091],
        [1.0000, 0.3717],
        [1.0000, 0.8436],
        [1.0000, 0.4544]], dtype=torch.float64)

Expected behavior
Type promotion should work correctly and the second assignment above should assign correct values.
Environment
pytorch master, linux, CPU (on fb infra)
cc @ezyang @gchanan @zou3519

import torch
from torch.distributions.categorical import Categorical

dev = torch.device('cuda')
